newsitem.title: USA: Neither Clinton nor Congress jumps at CPI change.
newsitem.headline: Neither Clinton nor Congress jumps at CPI change.

text.p: Overstating inflation is costing the U.S. government billions, some experts think, but change could be so politically painful that the White House and Congress appear to be saying to each other: You go first.
The experts' report announcing that government statistics were exaggerating inflation by 1.1 percentage points a year was unveiled with great fanfare on Wednesday on Capitol Hill.

As the handiwork of a panel of esteemed economists, including former White House economic adviser Michael Boskin, it would seem to give politicians the cover they need to fix the government inflation gauge, the Consumer Price Index, and take a big step toward balancing the federal budget.

The only problem is that scaling back the CPI would mean reducing Social Security pensions and other government benefits that are indexed to it. The move would also raise taxes for some Americans by lowering the levels at which higher tax rates take effect.

Sure, it might save the federal government plenty of money and help balance the budget. But if there's anything in Washington that's considered scarier than a tax increase, it's reducing the benefits that go to the elderly, a fast-growing group of Americans who vote in large numbers.

Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan, a New York Democrat who has long agitated for updating the inflation gauge, said the government could save $1 trillion in 10 years by changing the CPI and added: "Clearly, this is a matter to be addressed."
Sen. William Roth, a Delaware Republican whose Senate Finance Committee commissioned the economists' report, said he favoured holding hearings on the issue next year.

But others did not rush to embrace the idea. The leader of the Republicans in the Senate, Trent Lott, said he would like to see President Bill Clinton, a Democrat, address the question and spell out the need for the change.
"And I believe if he does that, we can work together and get that adjustment," Lott said.
At the White House, officials were studying the matter.

Larry Haas, a spokesman for the Office of Management and Budget, said that even if the administration decided it agreed with the Boskin commission, it was unlikely that it could do so in time for Clinton's budget submission due by Feb. 3.

"As a practical matter it does not seem reasonable to me that we would have time to make a careful study of the Boskin commission recommendations and incorporate any changes into the budget (for the next fiscal year)," Haas said.

Both Congress and the White House say they want to balance the federal budget over the next few years, and updating the inflation gauge would seem one way to do so. The economists' commission said the upward bias in the CPI would add $148 billion to the federal budget deficit by 2006 if not fixed.
Administration officials said the matter might come up as part of the budget negotiations with Congress later next year, but that Clinton would not get out in front on the issue.
"We're just not going to lead on it," one official said. Another said: "It may come up again and if it does we would have to see where the debate is and whether we'd want to sign on."

Officials also pointed out that there was a normal process of review by the agency that produces the inflation numbers, the Bureau of Labour Statistics. "Obviously changes could take place through that process," one official said, "so presumably if a consensus were to build that way we might be part of it."
But he said the White House could not order the bureau to change its inflation formula. "You don't mess with the numbers people."

BLS Commissioner Katharine Abraham said in a statement that there were clearly some differences of opinion between her office and the economists' panel. She said the BLS would be looking seriously at the recommendations "over the coming weeks and months."
